purpose: Niacin is used to help improve your cholesterol levels. It works by lowering your 'bad' cholesterol (LDL) and triglycerides while raising your 'good' cholesterol (HDL). Doctors may prescribe it to help reduce your risk of heart disease.
how_it_works: Niacin is a B vitamin that, in higher doses, acts like a medicine for your cholesterol. It tells your liver to make less bad cholesterol and more good cholesterol. Think of it as a natural traffic controller that redirects the fats in your blood in a healthier direction.
common_side_effects: The most common and well-known side effect is 'flushing' — a warm, red, tingling feeling on your skin, especially on your face and neck. This usually happens 30 to 60 minutes after taking the pill and gets better over time. You may also experience itching, headache, upset stomach, nausea, or dizziness.
warnings: Niacin can raise blood sugar levels, so it is especially important to monitor this if you have diabetes. It can also affect your liver, so avoid drinking alcohol while taking it, and your doctor will do regular blood tests to check your liver. Do not suddenly stop taking it without talking to your doctor. Tell your doctor if you have gout, ulcers, or kidney or liver problems before taking this medication.
typical_dosing: Doses vary depending on why you are taking it. For cholesterol, doses typically range from 500 mg to 2,000 mg per day, usually taken at bedtime to reduce flushing. Your doctor will likely start you on a low dose and slowly increase it. Taking an aspirin about 30 minutes before your dose can help reduce the flushing feeling. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
